reference.source: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology / EAU Guidelines on Urological Infections
clinicalPearls: Corresponds to NIH category II prostatitis and is defined by recurrent urinary tract infections caused by the same uropathogen, most often Escherichia coli and related Enterobacteriaceae, seeding from a persistent prostatic focus
Between symptomatic flares men may be well or have only low-grade perineal or pelvic discomfort, mild voiding symptoms, or post-ejaculatory pain
The prostate behaves as a protected reservoir in which organisms persist within ducts, biofilm and calcifications, which explains relapse after short antibiotic courses

Segmented localisation cultures, either the four-glass Meares-Stamey test or the simpler pre- and post-massage two-glass test, support a prostatic source when post-massage specimens grow markedly higher counts of the same organism
It is separated from chronic pelvic pain syndrome (NIH category III) by demonstrable bacterial growth localised to prostatic secretions
Management relies on a prolonged course of an antibiotic with good prostatic penetration guided by culture and sensitivity, rather than a brief course
Alpha-blockers, treatment of prostatic calculi and attention to sources of reinfection may reduce the relapse rate
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic bacterial prostatitis develops when ascending or intraprostatic infection establishes a persistent nidus, frequently within obstructed ducts, prostatic calculi, or areas of intraprostatic reflux of infected urine. The blood-prostate barrier and poor antibiotic penetration into non-inflamed prostatic tissue allow organisms to survive, and biofilm on prostatic stones shelters bacteria, producing the characteristic relapsing pattern of recurrent lower urinary tract infection with an identical organism.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (NIH category III prostatitis)
Benign prostatic enlargement with recurrent infection
Bladder outlet obstruction or incomplete emptying causing recurrent urinary tract infection
additionalInvestigations: Segmented localisation cultures (four-glass Meares-Stamey test or two-glass pre- and post-massage test)
Midstream urine culture during symptomatic episodes to identify the recurrent organism
Microscopy and culture of expressed prostatic secretions
Post-void residual measurement and uroflowmetry to assess for obstruction
Transrectal ultrasound or MRI when abscess or prostatic calculi are suspected
PSA interpreted with caution because prostatic inflammation can raise it
Sexually transmitted infection screening where urethritis is possible
redFlags: High fever, rigors or systemic sepsis suggesting acute prostatitis or a prostatic abscess
Failure to respond to appropriately targeted therapy, raising concern for abscess or a resistant organism
A rising PSA that does not settle after treatment, warranting exclusion of malignancy
reference.prognosis: Many men achieve cure or prolonged remission after an adequate, prolonged course of a prostate-penetrating antibiotic, but relapse is common, particularly when prostatic calculi harbour organisms, and some follow a chronic relapsing course requiring suppressive or repeated treatment.
pitfalls: Using short antibiotic courses that fail to achieve adequate prostatic penetration, leading to relapse
Not performing localisation cultures and so mislabelling abacterial category III disease as bacterial
Overlooking prostatic calculi as a reservoir of persistent infection
Attributing a raised PSA solely to prostatitis without arranging follow-up to exclude cancer
management: Treat with a prolonged course of an antibiotic that penetrates the prostate, such as a fluoroquinolone like ciprofloxacin or trimethoprim, guided by culture and sensitivity
Relieve voiding symptoms with an alpha-blocker and provide analgesia or anti-inflammatory drugs for pelvic and post-ejaculatory pain
Identify and address predisposing factors such as bladder-outlet obstruction and prostatic calculi that harbour organisms
Confirm the prostatic source and eradication with segmented localisation and follow-up cultures
Use low-dose suppressive antibiotic therapy or repeated culture-directed courses for the relapsing pattern
Consider surgical intervention such as transurethral resection to remove infected calculi in refractory relapsing disease, and drain any prostatic abscess
Refer to urology for recurrent or treatment-resistant disease
